catalog_quote: This study focusses on the stress system of the Northern dialect. Hess (1977:404) writes that the major stress in Northern Lushootseed words occurs on the first non-schwa of a stem, or, if all the vowels are schwas, on the first schwa. Hess also mentions that there seems to be a "sub-classs of lexical suffixes which receive primary stress regardless of preceding vowels." Yet, as we see in (1), there is significant variation in the placement of stress in Lushootseed and it can occur in every available (stressable) position. ... Kye 2023 covers both dialects and gives paired Northern/Southern forms.

new_statements.quote: In Lushootseed, there is at most one stressed syllable per word. Roots that are monosyllabic tend to be the location of primary stress in a word. [...] (1) reflects the pattern that occurs in the Southern dialect. However, in the Northern dialect, the location of primary stress is on the first non-schwa syllable of a stem. [p. 227] According to Hess (1977), stress tends to fall on the penultimate syllable in the Southern dialect. [p. 228] In short, word-level stress is predictable in Lushootseed. However, there are dialect-specific and word-specific differences that are not always predictable in a stem. [p. 230] Although there is a general tendency for the first full vowel of a stem to be stressed, this isn't the case for every word and every dialect in Lushootseed. [pp. 232-233]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog rule is empty (record from the quantity-sensitive tier of 2026-09-12). Kye's 'first full vowel of the stem' rule is a schwa-vs-full-vowel quality sensitivity, compatible with a quantity/quality-sensitive classification, and adds the stem domain, the Northern/Southern dialect split, the lexical-suffix interactions and the possible secondary stress. Kye's data come from Hess (1977), Urbanczyk (1996) and Bates et al. (1994), so this reading also represents what the listed dictionary encodes in its entries.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word, predictable and quality-sensitive within the stem: the first full (non-schwa) vowel of the stem is stressed; a monosyllabic root with a full vowel keeps stress even before a lexical suffix; a schwa root loses stress to a following full-vowel suffix syllable (Northern dialect: first non-schwa syllable of the stem, e.g. kʷəd-ˈad 'grab', təˈyil; Southern dialect: the root syllable is stressed even when it is schwa, ˈkʷəd-əd, ˈtəyil, with a penultimate tendency per Hess 1977, e.g. ˈgʷədbixʷ ~ gʷədˈbixʷ-ac). When root and lexical suffix both contain only schwa, stress falls on the first syllable of the stem (the root) in both dialects.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Kye p. 232: durational evidence (Figure 10.1) 'may suggest' a secondarily stressed syllable in words of three or more syllables; presented as possible, not established.
new_statements.exceptions: Dialect-specific (Northern vs Southern) and word-specific placements in root + lexical-suffix stems (some lexical suffixes pull stress from the root, others do not); Southern words that do not fit the penultimate pattern (Hess 1977: stʼiˈxʷibx̌, stʼəˈq̓axʷ); Urbanczyk (1996): preference for stressing the more sonorous /a/, so initial stress is forgone in about half of stems with /a/ in second position; a set of monosyllabic roots with 'reducible /a/' that becomes schwa before a full-vowel suffix.
new_statements.identity_note: Bates, Hess & Hilbert 1994 state that their data are predominantly Northern Lushootseed (Tulalip/Snohomish, Skagit incl. Swinomish, Sauk-Suiattle); Southern Lushootseed (Skykomish, Snoqualmie, Suquamish, Duwamish, Muckleshoot, Puyallup, Nisqually, Sahewamish) has a different stress pattern. Kye 2023 covers both dialects and gives paired Northern/Southern forms.

readall_conflicts: No source contradicts another. The dictionary's open pages say only that Northern and Southern Lushootseed have different stress patterns; Kye 2023 supplies what those patterns are (Northern: first non-schwa syllable of the stem; Southern: the root syllable even when schwa, with a penultimate tendency reported by Hess 1977). The label is a judgement call between 'weight-sensitive' (full vowel vs schwa decides) and 'morphologically determined' (stress stays inside the root/stem and defaults to the root when only schwas are present); Kye's own summary ('general tendency for the first full vowel of a stem to be stressed') puts vowel quality first, so weight-sensitive is chosen, with the stem domain and dialect split recorded in the rule. Kye also stresses that some root + lexical-suffix stems have dialect- or word-specific placements that the rule does not predict.

(2) The deciding source is a short 1995 conference working paper formalising Hess 1977's descriptive rule; better descriptions exist (Kye 2023 UW dissertation, Urbanczyk 1996).
